title: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two last-in-first-out stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue, and analyse the amortised cost.
shortTitle: Implement a Queue Using Two Stacks
keyPoints: Push to an inbox stack; pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty; pop outbox for dequeue.
Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortized O(1) per operation.
Lazy transfer (only when outbox is empty) is what preserves both FIFO order and amortized complexity.
Eager transfer on every dequeue destroys the ordering and the amortized guarantee.
This pattern appears in functional data structures as the Banker's queue with two lists.
In production Java, use ArrayDeque directly; the two-stack queue is for constrained environments.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push to an inbox stack, pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty, and each element moves once for amortized constant time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-stack queue** – simulate FIFO using two LIFO stacks: an inbox for enqueue and an outbox for dequeue.
- **Lazy transfer** – pour the inbox into the outbox only when the outbox is empty, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top.
- **Amortized O(1)** – each element is pushed to inbox once, moved to outbox once, and popped once over its lifetime.
- **Eager transfer** – transferring on every dequeue breaks both ordering and complexity.
- **Banker's queue** – the functional data structures equivalent uses two lists in place of two stacks.
- **Production** – in real Java, use `ArrayDeque` as a queue; the two-stack construction is for stack-only environments.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture two spikes at the National Bank of India teller window. New request slips go onto the incoming spike. When the teller wants to serve the next customer in fairness order, she checks the serving spike. If it is empty she flips the whole incoming pile onto it, reversing the order so the earliest arrival is on top. She serves from the serving spike until it empties, then flips again only when needed.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Two-Stack Queue
  ───────────────

  enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C):

  Inbox          Outbox
  ┌─────┐        ┌─────┐
  │  C  │ top    │     │ empty
  ├─────┤        └─────┘
  │  B  │
  ├─────┤
  │  A  │
  └─────┘

  dequeue() → outbox empty → transfer:

  Inbox          Outbox
  ┌─────┐        ┌─────┐
  │     │ empty  │  A  │ top  (oldest!)
  └─────┘        ├─────┤
                 │  B  │
                 ├─────┤
                 │  C  │
                 └─────┘

  outbox.pop() → A (FIFO)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A queue from two stacks works by pushing to an inbox and serving from an outbox. When the outbox is empty, I pour the entire inbox into it, reversing the order so the oldest element is on top. Each element moves between stacks at most once in its lifetime, giving amortized O(1) per operation.

The lazy transfer rule is what makes this efficient. Transferring only when the outbox is empty ensures each element moves exactly once. Eager transfer on every dequeue breaks both the FIFO ordering and the amortized guarantee, because newly enqueued elements get mixed with older ones.

Explaining the amortized analysis, that worst-case O(n) for one call does not mean O(n) per operation on average, is the real point of this interview question. Each element pays a constant total cost across its lifetime: one push to inbox, one move to outbox, one pop from outbox.

In my project at the National Bank of India, a legacy component exposed only stack primitives, but customer service requests needed strict oldest-first fairness. The two-stack queue gave FIFO semantics, and the lazy transfer kept throughput high during burst processing. In production Java I would use `ArrayDeque` directly, but the two-stack construction is exactly the Banker's queue from functional data structures.

Remember one sentence: push to inbox, pour into outbox only when empty, and each element moves at most once for amortized O(1).
